17.0.0.en: Paul and Silas left Philippi and journeyed on foot for a day, and reached the city of Amphipolis. They did not stay there either, because there was no Jewish synagogue there, for Paul used to take the Jews as the starting point of his preaching and evangelizing. Then they travelled for a third day and reached Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia in the north of Greece, a well-known port.

17.1.0.en: The Scriptures: the books of the Old Testament.

17.1.1.en: Paul and Silas entered the synagogue, as was their custom, to preach first to the Jews. Although Paul was the apostle of the Gentiles, he cared for the Jews, besides using them as an entrance for evangelizing the Gentiles, some of whom attended the Jewish synagogue. They continued preaching for three Sabbaths in the synagogue, but they remained in the city for a longer time than this, during which St. Paul worked at the trade of tent-making (2 Thess 3:8), and there financial help reached them from Philippi twice.

17.2.0.en: St. Paul proved from the prophecies the necessity of the suffering of the expected Messiah, then His resurrection and His kingship, and this is what happened with Jesus; therefore Jesus is the Christ. For the Jews thought that the Messiah would be a king who would free them from the Romans, so they rejected the idea of His suffering and death, as the prophecies had said.

17.3.0.en: Consorted with: they joined in the faith of Paul and Silas, that is, they became members of the Church of Thessalonica. Some of the Jews believed, and many of the devout Greeks, who used to pray in the synagogue without becoming proselytes to Judaism, and also some of the women married to men of high position.

17.4.0.en: The lewd fellows of the baser sort (the market people): idle men who sit in the marketplace, Gentiles of the lowest classes. The Jews exploited them to stir up the Gentiles of the city, because they were Gentiles like them.

17.4.1.en: Set the city on an uproar: they stirred up the city with doubts against the teaching of Paul and Silas.

17.4.2.en: Jason: a Jew who believed the preaching of Paul and was his kinsman according to the flesh, and he hosted Paul and Silas in his house.

17.4.3.en: The Jews felt that faith in God and His blessings belonged to them alone, so they were greatly troubled when the Gentiles believed in God as they did. They hired wicked men to stir up the city and make it doubt Paul's preaching, and they attacked the house of Jason, Paul's kinsman, searching for the two Apostles.

17.5.0.en: The rulers of the city: Thessalonica was a free city, which Caesar allowed to be governed by men from among its own people, who had the authority to punish and to put to death.

17.5.1.en: Troubled: stirred up and disturbed with strange teachings.

17.5.2.en: They did not find Paul and Silas in the house of Jason, so they seized him and some of the Christians and took them to the rulers, and accused Paul and Silas of spreading strange teachings everywhere, and said that they had come to Thessalonica and begun to spread their teachings.

17.6.0.en: As usual, they mixed the religious accusation with a political one, claiming that Paul and Silas had taught against Caesar and proclaimed that Jesus is a king, and that Jason had hosted them in his house.

17.7.0.en: The people and the rulers were disturbed by this, and feared Caesar's revenge upon the city.

17.8.0.en: The rulers took a sum of money from Jason as a guarantee that he would send Paul and Silas out of the city, then released him and the Christians who had been seized. This shows the justice of these rulers and that they did not rush along behind the wicked Jews.

17.8.1.en: Do not stir up others against those who oppose you, and be careful in your speech lest you ascribe to them faults that are not in them. Rather, respect the opinion of others even if it differs from yours, and let God do what He wills even if it is against your opinion, for your agitation and anger will change nothing in the ordering of God's will, but will only increase your sins and your tension. Care only for your inner peace and for peace in your relationships with others.

17.9.0.en: Immediately: on the evening of the same day as the trial, so that things in the city might calm down, the rulers be reassured, and the uproar of the Jews subside.

17.9.1.en: Berea: it lies southwest of Thessalonica in the province of Macedonia, and the number of Jews in it is smaller than in Thessalonica.

17.9.2.en: The Christians sent Paul and Silas to Berea by night so that the Jews would not see them and harm them, and there the two Apostles began preaching in the synagogue of the Jews.

17.10.0.en: More noble: loftier in mind, understanding and breadth of heart.

17.10.1.en: With all readiness of mind: eagerness to understand what they had heard and to apply it in their lives.

17.10.2.en: Whether those things were so: making sure of the truth of the faith they had heard, with proofs from the prophecies found in the books of the Old Testament, so as to confirm this faith.

17.10.3.en: The Jews of Berea were better than the Jews of Thessalonica in their care to examine the prophecies and the Holy Scriptures, as the Lord said, "Search the scriptures" (Jn 5:39).

17.11.0.en: Many of the Jewish men believed, and of the Greek women who had joined the Jews, women of high rank, and also many of the Greek men.

17.12.0.en: The Jews of Thessalonica were enraged when they learned that the faith had spread in Berea, so they sent men from among them to stir up the people of Berea against Paul and Silas.

17.13.0.en: The Christians hastened to send Paul away as though he would travel by sea, in order to calm the anger of the Jews, but he travelled by land to Athens, the capital of Greece, although the land route is much longer. Silas and Timothy remained in Berea to complete the ministry, since the eyes of the wicked Jews were fixed on Paul and not on his companions.

17.13.1.en: Thus Paul ended his ministry in Macedonia, which was concentrated in three important places, Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, as the divine vision had called him to serve in Macedonia (ch. 16:9); and afterward the Spirit of God directed him to serve in Athens, the center of Greek philosophy.

17.14.0.en: A group of the Christians of Berea accompanied Paul, and after arranging a place of residence for him in Athens, they returned to Berea and informed Silas and Timothy that Paul was waiting for them in Athens, so they travelled to him quickly.

17.14.1.en: Let your goal, which is the love of Christ and being with Him in eternity, always be before your eyes, and if obstacles confront you, flee from them and continue looking toward your goal. Do not be disturbed by opposition, for the devil is weak; he stirs up troubles, but he cannot stop your love and your striving toward God.

17.15.0.en: Paul was in Athens waiting for the arrival of Silas and Timothy, but he was troubled by the abundance of licentiousness in the pagan worship that was so widespread in the city, so that the historian Petronius said: it is easier to find a god in Athens than to find a man in it.

17.16.0.en: Paul preached only to the Jews in the synagogue and in the marketplace, because it was not only a place for buying and selling; many people gathered in it for dialogue and discussion.

17.17.0.en: Epicureans: followers of Epicurus, the Roman philosopher who appeared in the third century B.C., who neglected the idea of divinity, proclaimed that there is no reward or punishment, and permitted indulgence in desires. Stoics: followers of Zeno, the Greek philosopher who appeared in the third century before Christ, who proclaimed the importance of reason and considered God to be the world. He used to deliver his teachings in a portico, and his followers were called Stoics and were distinguished by pride.

17.17.1.en: St. Paul met a group of Greek philosophers belonging to the Epicureans and the Stoics, who thought that he was proclaiming strange gods because he was proclaiming Jesus and the resurrection from the dead. They supposed that he was proclaiming two gods, Jesus and the Resurrection, so they despised him and described him as a babbler, that is, one who does not understand what he says.

17.18.0.en: Areopagus: the highest philosophical council in Athens, in which they met to examine the various philosophies, ancient and modern.

17.18.1.en: These philosophers asked Paul to come with them to the council of the Areopagus, which met in a tiered place on the hill, to hear his new teaching, the like of which they had not heard before, so that they might examine this philosophy and decide whether it was right or wrong, and accordingly permit him to continue this teaching or stop it.

17.19.0.en: The most important thing to the people of Athens and its visitors was continual philosophical discussion, especially of new philosophies and ideas such as this new teaching that Paul was teaching.

17.19.1.en: Would that we spent our time on what is useful and not on vain talk. Avoid discussions that are of no benefit or that cause you to fall into mistaken ideas, and present Christ in your words and deeds in the form of love for those around you.

17.20.0.en: Paul began his sermon in the greatest philosophical council in Athens, which was famous throughout the whole world for its advancement in knowledge and philosophy at that time. He began by saying that he saw the great religiousness of the people of Athens, evident from the multitude of their idols. In this he commends a virtue in them, namely the religious inclination, even if it was in a mistaken direction, for it was a clear interest in religion, and this was in order to win their hearts to listen to him.

17.21.0.en: While Paul was passing through the streets of the city and getting to know its gods, he saw among their objects of worship one they called an unknown god. For a plague had spread in the city, and one of the philosophers advised them to release sheep throughout the city, and wherever a sheep lay down at the altar of any god, they were to offer it to that god to appease him. When some of the sheep lay down in places where there were no altars, they built altars and called them to an unknown god. Paul told them that he had come to preach to them the God whom they fear, for dread of His wrath, without knowing Him. By this he escaped the charge of preaching a new religion.

17.22.0.en: Paul said that this God is the one God, the Creator of the whole world, and that He is too great to dwell in temples built with hands, as St. Stephen had said in his speech before his martyrdom (ch. 7:48-50). This teaching is not against the presence of God in the tabernacle of meeting or the temple of Solomon in the Old Testament, or His presence in the Church of the New Testament, for He dwells there with His blessing, but His presence is not confined to them; rather He dwells in heaven and fills every place. In this Paul proclaims the oneness of God, and this is against the beliefs of the pagans in Athens.

17.23.0.en: Paul proclaimed that God has no need of the service and gifts of men, because He is the giver of life and of all blessings; but the offering of worship to God, in the Old or the New Testament, is a declaration of man's repentance, love and thanksgiving to Him.

17.24.0.en: Paul also proclaimed that God is the Creator of all from one origin, so there is no distinction between one race and another, but all are brothers, whom God distributed over the earth to inhabit it, each in the place and time suited to him, and He determined when a nation rises and when another falls. In this he rejects the arrogance of the Greeks toward the rest of mankind.

17.25.0.en: St. Paul asked them to seek God and establish a relationship with Him, for He is very near to them, not only with them but dwelling within them.

17.26.0.en: Paul made clear that God is the source of the life of all mankind, and he confirmed his words with sayings of the Greek poets, such as the Greek poet Aratus in 277 B.C. and the poet Cleanthes in 300 B.C., that we are His offspring. This shows St. Paul's study of Greek culture in Tarsus, in addition to his religious study at the feet of Gamaliel, the great teacher of the Jews. By this he proclaimed that God is very near to man, and not, as the Greeks think, that the gods dwell in distant places and are separate from mankind, or that matter came into being by itself.

17.27.0.en: The Apostle concluded from the sayings of the Greek poets that we are like God, as His offspring, so we know that the Godhead is not material but spiritual, like our spirits, which are in His likeness. If the essence of man is distinct from lifeless matter, then all the more the essence of God (the Godhead) is far higher than lifeless matter, that is, the idols. It is to be noticed that Paul did not rely in his proofs on verses of the Holy Scriptures, but on the sayings of pagan poets and philosophers, to persuade them to believe in God.

17.28.0.en: Now: since the preaching of the Gospel has begun in the whole world, as our Lord Jesus Christ commanded. All men: Jews and Gentiles.

17.28.1.en: Ignorance: he did not speak of evil and disobedience to God, but pleads an excuse for them, that they were idolaters through ignorance, and this is a gentle way of drawing the hearers to faith.

17.28.2.en: God calls all men to repentance, and promises them the forgiveness of their sins.

17.29.0.en: The world: all mankind, Jews and Gentiles.

17.29.1.en: In righteousness: without partiality or discrimination of race or person.

17.29.2.en: Whereof He hath given assurance unto all men: Christ accomplished redemption on the Cross, and offers salvation through preaching about Him, that men may believe and be saved.

17.29.3.en: Paul proclaimed the necessity of repentance, because God has appointed a day of judgment, on which He will send a man to judge all mankind, and he is Christ, whom He raised from the dead.

17.30.0.en: Some mocked: they were the Epicureans, who were immersed in desires and did not believe in the day of judgment, so they mocked Paul's teachings.

17.30.1.en: Others said, We will hear thee again of this matter: the others were the Stoics, who were more dignified and more receptive to faith in God. These asked to hear more details from him about this teaching, but they went back and rejected his teachings when they examined them, because they found them against their beliefs.

17.30.2.en: Despite the multiplicity of the religions of Athens, they all agreed that there is no resurrection after death, so when they heard the mention of the resurrection they mocked Paul, especially the Epicureans among them, and asked to postpone the rest of the talk to another time.

17.31.0.en: Departed: the council passed no judgment on him, but the majority of them rejected his teachings, as shown by his leaving free.

17.31.1.en: Dionysius: a Greek philosopher who was studying philosophy in Egypt at the time of the crucifixion of Christ, and saw the darkness that occurred at the sixth hour, that is, at noon, and said, as a student of astronomy, that this means that the God of the world is suffering. Then he returned to Greece and joined their philosophical council, the Areopagus, and when he heard Paul's teachings he believed in Christ. He has a homily (address) that is sometimes read on Great Friday. Paul departed from among them, and those who believed clave to him, among them a member of the philosophical council of the Areopagus, which required its members to be former judges over sixty years of age, whose name was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

17.31.2.en: Paul presented his message although many rejected it, but few accepted the faith.

17.31.3.en: Offer your love to all who are around you, even if many reject it, for some may accept it, and the rest may be affected after a while.

17.31.4.en: The ministry in Corinth and the end of the second journey

18.0.s.en: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

18.0.0.en: Paul left Athens because he did not expect success in preaching there, and came to Corinth in the province of Hellas at the far south of Greece. It had a port on the east and another on the west, because it was the largest city in the south of Greece, which was called Achaia, just as Thessalonica was the largest city in the north, which was called Macedonia. In Corinth there was a temple for the worship of Venus, with a thousand priestesses who practiced vice with the worshippers of the temple as part of the worship. This shows the extent of the moral decay of this city, yet Paul remained in it a year and a half (v. 11), and the preaching succeeded greatly in it, and from it he wrote his two epistles to the Thessalonians.

18.1.0.en: In Corinth there was a Christian of Jewish origin named Aquila, and with him his wife Priscilla.

18.1.1.en: They were originally from Pontus in northeastern Turkey, and were among the Jews whom Claudius Caesar had expelled from Rome, for he commanded the expulsion of all the Jews of Rome and forbade any Jew to live there because of the many disturbances that the Jews stirred up. So Paul came to them.

18.2.0.en: The Jews were accustomed to teach their children a trade, whatever their educational and cultural level. So although Saul of Tarsus had learned philosophy and the religious sciences, he had trained in the trade of tent-making. When he visited Corinth and found Aquila and his wife working at the same trade, that encouraged him to stay with them and share this work with them, so as not to depend on anyone for the expenses of his living.

18.3.0.en: St. Paul used to go every Sabbath to preach, discuss and persuade the Jews and the Greek proselytes in the synagogue concerning Christianity; on the other days he worked at tent-making, and he spent Sunday in spiritual worship with the Christians Aquila and Priscilla who were in Corinth.

18.4.0.en: Pressed in spirit: with zeal and great fervor.

18.4.1.en: When Silas and Timothy, who had been in Macedonia in the north of Greece in the city of Thessalonica, came to Paul, he was preaching in Corinth to show the Jews that Jesus is the Christ, the Savior.

18.5.0.en: The Jews opposed Paul with harsh words against Christ, so he shook his garments, as a sign of God's abandoning of the obstinate, and held them responsible for their rejection, declaring that he was innocent of their blood and that he would begin to preach to the Gentiles.

18.6.0.en: Paul moved to the house of a man named Justus, next to the synagogue. He was one of the Greeks who worship God without becoming proselytes, and he had accepted faith in Christ. Paul took his house as a place from which to teach those who believed or were coming to the faith, because this house was suitable for that, being next to the synagogue, so everyone knew it and it was easy for them to meet with him.

18.7.0.en: Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, had believed, he and his household, and St. Paul baptized him (1 Cor 1:14). This helped many Jews to enter the faith, and also the Greeks who were interested in the worship of God, for they came to hear Paul's teachings, and believed and were baptized. Thus the ministry succeeded greatly in a very wicked city, and this is proof of the work of God, who never lets us despair of doing good.

18.8.0.en: I am with thee: since he feels that God is with him, he is reassured and encouraged to preach with zeal and to endure the opposition of the wicked, assured by God's promise that they cannot harm him or stop his preaching. I have much people: many souls will believe in Christ.

18.8.1.en: The Lord appeared to Paul in a vision to encourage him not to fear the violence of the opposition of the Jews of Corinth or the disdain of the Greeks there who were occupied with their desires, and to encourage him to continue preaching, declaring that He would keep him from all evil, because many would believe.

18.9.0.en: Paul continued preaching Christianity for a year and a half, and founded a church there and organized its worship and responsibilities. He cared about this city because it is a port where many people coming from Rome, Alexandria and Ephesus meet, besides being an important city in the province of Achaia, that is, southern Greece.

18.9.1.en: When the wicked oppose you, do not despair and give up, for God supports you and He is stronger than all, knowing that some people do not accept the truth except after a long time, yet they may become stronger than the rest in their life with God.

18.10.0.en: Achaia: the Romans divided Greece into a northern province which they called Macedonia, and a southern one which they called Achaia, whose capital is Corinth, where the seat of the governorship was.

18.10.1.en: The judgment seat: it was customary for governors to sit on a seat of their own in a large square in the city to examine the cases and problems of the people.

18.10.2.en: The law: by it they mean the law of the Jews recognized by the Romans, and consequently preaching another religion under the name of Judaism was against Roman laws. It is possible that by the law they meant the Roman laws.

18.10.3.en: Gallio became proconsul of Achaia, who was the brother of the famous Roman philosopher Seneca, and he was a just man. At that time the Jews rose up with great violence against Paul and brought him to the governor's palace to be tried on a grave charge, namely that he was preaching a new religion not recognized by the Roman state, as Judaism was recognized by the Romans, a charge that led to expulsion or death.

18.11.0.en: Wrong: that is, depriving others of their rights and assaulting them.

18.11.1.en: Wicked lewdness: an evil intent that has evidence and leads to injustice.

18.11.2.en: Gallio did not wait for Paul to defend himself, but thought, as the Romans thought, that Christianity was a sect of Judaism, and that the problems of Christianity with the Jews were internal religious problems in which the Romans do not judge, but the Jews themselves. So Gallio declared to the Jews that this dispute was not within his competence, because it was a dispute about words and Jewish names, for Paul calls Jesus the Christ and they do not accept that, and he told them to judge him in their synagogue in a religious manner, where the greatest penalty would be to be cut off from the synagogue. But Gallio did not know that he had lost the opportunity of saving his own soul when he did not understand Paul's preaching, while the Lord delivered Paul from the Jewish plot.

18.12.0.en: Gallio drove the Jews away and rejected their case, especially since they were hated by the Greeks and the Romans because of their many troubles.

18.13.0.en: Gallio cared for none of those things: he allowed the pagans to beat Sosthenes to vent their anger, although this was contrary to the laws, but of course it was within certain limits. This shows his neglect of Jewish religious cases, for they were not his work as governor.

18.13.1.en: The Greeks of the people of Corinth seized the opportunity of the anger of Gallio the governor against the Jews, and beat Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue of the Jews, to humiliate them. The Jews had appointed Sosthenes ruler of their synagogue in succession to Crispus, who had believed in Christianity. But after this we read in (1 Cor 1:1) that Sosthenes also believed and accompanied St. Paul in his preaching.

18.13.2.en: Do not fear the plots of the wicked, for God is able to deliver you from them as He delivered Paul, however difficult the circumstances may appear, or however continuous the accusations and unceasing the insults, for in the end God turns all this to your good and keeps your inner peace, and even rewards you in eternity for what you endured.

18.14.s.en: (3) The end of the second journey

18.14.0.en: Tarried there yet: after the agitation of the Jews against him calmed down, he continued for a time preaching in Corinth.

18.14.1.en: The brethren: the believers in Corinth.

18.14.2.en: Paul completed his preaching in Corinth for some time after that, then bade them farewell, returning to Syria. He had a vow upon him for a personal reason, according to the custom of the Law, for the Christians of Jewish origin such as Paul used to keep the commandments of the Law which they had been accustomed to throughout their lives before the faith, except the rites that were a type of Christ, such as the sacrifices.

18.14.3.en: After the period of the vow ended, Paul shaved his head, as is the custom of Nazirites, and this was in Cenchrea (the port of Corinth on its eastern side) (Num 6:1-21). Paul fulfilled the Mosaic law so as not to cause the Jews to stumble, although he did not require the Gentiles to keep it, because it is not necessary for obtaining salvation. Paul took Priscilla and Aquila with him. Here we see that the name of the wife is put before that of her husband, which shows the strength of her faith and her ministry.

18.15.0.en: Ephesus: the capital of Asia Minor (Turkey), an important port about three days from Corinth.

18.15.1.en: Left them there: he left Aquila and Priscilla to complete the preaching and ministry in Ephesus.

18.15.2.en: Entered into the synagogue: he was not troubled by the opposition of the Jews to him in Corinth, but continued to love them and began to preach to them in Ephesus that they might believe in Christ.

18.15.3.en: They all arrived at Ephesus in Turkey, and Paul left Aquila and his wife there, and entered the synagogue to preach and discuss with the Jews as was his custom.

18.16.0.en: The Jews in Ephesus responded to Paul's sermons and asked him to stay with them and complete his preaching among them, but he did not agree; rather he travelled, because he wanted to attend the coming feast of Pentecost in Jerusalem to complete the procedures of his vow and burn the hair he had shaved in the temple, and so that he could preach to the Jews gathered in Jerusalem at the feast of Pentecost, who had come to it from all parts of the world. He promised the people of Ephesus to return to them on his coming (third) journey, and indeed he returned and stayed with them three years (ch. 20:31).

18.17.0.en: Caesarea: it is considered the port of Jerusalem, that is, the nearest port to it.

18.17.1.en: Paul arrived by sea from Ephesus at Caesarea in Palestine, then from there to Jerusalem to greet the Church and the Apostles and tell them what had happened on his second journey. This was his fourth visit to Jerusalem. Then he returned to Antioch for the last time, to rest a little before beginning his third journey, on which he set out from Antioch, and he did not return to it for the rest of his life on earth.

18.17.2.en: His second journey lasted three years (from A.D. 51 to 54).

18.17.3.en: What great striving Paul accomplished!... May your life be as fruitful for the Lord.

18.17.4.en: Do you use all your time in useful things? May your goal, which is the love of Christ, always be before your eyes, that it may give you zeal for spiritual work.

18.18.s.en: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

18.18.0.en: Galatia and Phrygia: two regions in Asia Minor, which is Turkey.

18.18.1.en: Paul stayed in Antioch for less than a year, then began his third missionary journey, as usual in Turkey and then Europe. The journey took the period from A.D. 54 to 58, and is recorded from (ch. 18:23) to (ch. 21:17). The route of the journey was as follows:

18.18.2.en: From Antioch (Syria) by land to Tarsus (Turkey), then by land to Derbe (Turkey), and after that by land to Iconium (Turkey) and from there by land to Antioch (Turkey). From there he went by sea to Ephesus (Turkey), where the riot of Demetrius and the craftsmen took place. From there he went by sea to Mitylene (Turkey), then by sea to Troas (Turkey), and after that by sea to Philippi (Greece). Then by land to Thessalonica (Greece), and from there he went by sea to Corinth in the province of Hellas (southern Greece), and from there by land to Berea (Greece), and from there he went by sea to Philippi (Greece), then by sea to Troas (Turkey), where the Apostle Paul raised the young man Eutychus from death. After that he went by land to Assos (Turkey), and from there by sea to Mitylene (Turkey), and after it by sea to Samos (Turkey), then by sea to Miletus (Turkey), and from there he sailed by sea to Cos (Turkey), and afterward went by sea to Rhodes (Greece), and after it by sea to Tyre (Palestine), and from there he went by land to Caesarea (Palestine), and finally arrived by land at Jerusalem.

18.19.0.en: Before Paul reached Ephesus, where he had earlier left Aquila and Priscilla, a Christian of Jewish origin named Apollos came to it. He was one of the Jews of Alexandria, gifted in discussion and a student of the Old Testament.

18.20.0.en: Mighty: deeply versed and living the spiritual meanings.

18.20.1.en: The way of the Lord: Christianity.

18.20.2.en: Fervent in spirit: full of zeal and spiritual power.

18.20.3.en: The baptism of John: the teachings of John, his baptizing of the people, and his witness to Christ.

18.20.4.en: Apollos was a spiritual man, who lived what he said and felt, but he knew nothing of Christianity except the witness of John the Baptist about Christ, and likewise he knew nothing of His teachings, His death and His resurrection.

18.21.0.en: It seems that Aquila and Priscilla were accustomed to attend the synagogue, so they heard Apollos preaching in it and discovered his knowledge of the death and resurrection of Christ, so they took him to them and expounded to him the rest of Christianity accurately. They spoke to him of the Cross, the Resurrection, redemption, the descent of the Holy Spirit and the Sacraments, and he listened humbly although he was a great orator and philosopher, and believed everything.

18.22.0.en: Apollos went to Corinth, the capital of Achaia in the south of Greece, to preach in it, and the Christians of Ephesus gave him a letter of recommendation to the believers in Corinth so that they would receive him without apprehension, and this was customary among the churches. So he strengthened the faith of the believers and answered the opposing Jews, and this helped in the steadfastness of the Church there.

18.23.0.en: Apollos proved to the Jews of Corinth that Jesus is the Christ from the prophecies and books of the Old Testament, and answered their opposition and silenced them, because he was filled with the Holy Spirit and had studied the science of rhetoric and persuasion in the school of Alexandria.

18.23.1.en: Every person has a gift that he ought to use for the service of Christ, like Apollos. So try to discover your gifts by prayer and the guidance of your father of confession, and use them for the benefit of the Church; you are responsible for investing them and you will be called to account for that, and at the same time you will enjoy the blessings of this gift for the growth of your life together with the others who benefit from it.
